name: Celery seed
short: Celery tuber allergy can cause fatal anaphylaxis; seed allergen data are scarce. Case report: severe phototoxic burn after eating celery root, then tanning. Seed trial: side effects like placebo.
text: None of the cited allergy or photosensitivity sources is stated to involve celery seed taken as a supplement: the fatal-anaphylaxis statement and the phototoxic burn concern celery tuber (root), and the other sources do not say which part of the plant people were exposed to. A laboratory study of two patients with an allergic reaction after eating a sauce (the abstract does not say whether it contained celery tuber or seed) states that celery tuber allergy is frequent in Central Europe and can cause allergic reactions including fatal anaphylactic shock, notes that there is little information about allergen content in seeds, and found distinct protein patterns in tuber and seed extracts, suggesting differences in the content and quantity of allergenic proteins; a separate case report describes food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis in the celery-mugwort-birch-spice syndrome. Celery contains furocoumarins and psoralens that can cause phytophotodermatitis with UV exposure; a review states that a typical dietary amount is generally insufficient, but that people who handle celery often, eat fungus-infected produce or use tanning beds are at higher risk, and a case report described a severe, generalised phototoxic reaction in a 65-year-old woman who visited a suntan parlour an hour after eating a large amount of celery root. For seed extract taken by mouth as capsules, two reports of a 4-week triple-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in people with high blood pressure (51 and 52 participants, with the same design; the abstracts do not say whether they are the same trial) were published: in the first, the capsules were taken as a supplement to usual medicines and the authors described the extract as safe, with no significant change in blood cells or serum electrolytes; the second reported no significant side effects compared with placebo; and a meta-analysis of ten randomised trials (511 adults) of various celery preparations found no significant difference in adverse events compared with placebo. The trials were small and short. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
